name: Auna Kambari
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Stark, Janie P. 2010. Kambari Orthography Design. SIL e-Books 16. Dallas: SIL International. xiv+227 pp. (revision of the 2000 University of Ilorin PhD thesis; description explicitly based on the Tsikimba dialect of Auna town, called 'Auna Kambari' in the book)
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.3.1.5 'Tone patterns', pp. 61-62; Sec. 2.3.1.4 'Syllable and word patterns', pp. 59-60; Appendix B 'Auna orthography', headings 'Unstressed /u/' p. 200 and 'Tone' p. 203; identity of variety p. 40 and p. 196)
catalog_quote: [p. 61] Lexical tone is demonstrated by pairs of words that differ only in their tonal value. Lexical tone in Kambari carries a very small semantic load. The following tone data indicates Kambari utilizes two level lexical tones. All the examples are in Auna Kambari, but the patterns are the same in the other two languages unless otherwise noted. ... On two-syllable nouns: LL [kala] 'name' HH No HH nouns occur HL ... 'open ridge' LH ... 'arrow' ... [p. 62] No other tone patterns are found on three-syllable nouns. Salka Kambari has the constraint that no word begins with a high tone. ... On verbs (in the simplest form): The citation form of verbs is the imperative. The imperative is nearly always LH. ... It should be noted that for each of the Kambari languages, minimal pairs that diverge only by tone are rare. ... [p. 200, Appendix B, Auna orthography] Unstressed /u/ When a suffix is added to the root, the last vowel of the root is replaced with /u/. In this position, the vowel does not receive the same length and “importance” as the same vowel in other positions. ... [p. 203] Auna Kambari has a small number of minimal tone pairs (under 20). Most of the minimal pairs are in different domains, so there is little possibility of confusion when reading. ... Tone is not written.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (241 pp; Stark, Janie P. 2010, Kambari Orthography Design, SIL e-Books 16). (1) Locator p. 61 = p. 75, sec. 2.3.1.5 'Tone patterns': text reads exactly 'Lexical tone is demonstrated by pairs of words that differ only in their tonal value. Lexical tone in Kambari carries a very small semantic load. The following tone data indicates Kambari utilizes two level lexical tones. All the examples are in Auna Kambari, but the patterns are the same in the other two languages unless otherwise noted.' followed by noun patterns LL/HL/LH (no HH), LLL/LHL/LHH/HLL/HHH, imperative verbs 'nearly always LH' (exception zama LL), Salka bars word-initial H, fn. 21 tone elicited in isolation -- all…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tsikimba (Auna Kambari) is described as a two-level-tone language with light lexical tone load (nouns LL/HL/LH, LLL/LHL/LHH/HLL/HHH; imperative verbs nearly always LH). The source gives no rule for the position of word stress; its only stress-related remark is that the root-final vowel becomes a reduced ('unstressed') /u/ ~ [ɨ]-like vowel when a suffix follows.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. For tone: Salka Kambari (not Tsikimba) disallows word-initial H; imperative verbs LH with a few LL exceptions (zama 'search').
new_statements.domain_note: Tone data elicited on isolated words (fn. 21, p. 61). The 'Unstressed /u/' remark concerns suffixed verb forms (root + iterative -sV etc.), i.e. word-internal vowel reduction, not phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Stark 2010 states (p. 40; App. B p. 196) that her 'Auna Kambari' description 'is based on the Tsikimba dialect as is spoken in Auna town' = tsik1238 / ISO kdl (other Auna Kambari dialects named: Tsishen, Tsugaunshi/Tsugaunshe). The same book also treats Agwara Kambari (Cishingini, asg) and Salka Kambari (Tsishingini, tsw, tsis1238) as co-languages; tone patterns are said to be shared except that Salka bars word-initial H. Glottolog's descriptive refs filed under tsik1238 (Hoffmann 1963, 1972 'Central Kambari') actually concern the Salka/Raba variety (tsis1238), so Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description for Tsikimba is effectively Stark 2010.

new_statements.quote: [p. 52] The phonological presentation is illustrated with Agwara Kambari data. ... [p. 59] The language has 2 contrastive tone levels. ... [p. 60] There is a small functional load for tone in Kambari. The mother-tongue speaker has a sense of ‘normal’ tone patterns for a word, similar to the sense of proper stress placement in English. ... [p. 61] Each syllable has a single tone; since VV is a single syllable no tone combinations can occur to produce falling or rising tone. Such an analysis also conforms to the stress/timing factors of the language, where the majority of VV occurrences receive a single stress with slight temporal length, yet a few VV occurrences receive two stress realizations.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Janie P. Stark 2010: two level lexical tones, small semantic load, no word-stress placement statement): same analysis ('2 contrastive tone levels', 'small functional load for tone'), evidently the shared KLP analysis. Adds only a phonetic 'stress/timing' remark about VV sequences (p. 61) that gives no placement rule, so the reading stays tone language, no stress statement. Identity: the chapter describes 'Kambari' as common to the three co-languages and illustrates with Agwara (Cishingini [asg]) data, not Tsikimba data; the author states the claims hold for all three (p. 52), so it bears on Auna Kambari only at that level of generality.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kambari (stated as common to Cishingini, Tsikimba = Auna Kambari, and Tsishingini; examples from Agwara/Cishingini) has two contrastive level tones (noun patterns LL, HL, LHL, LLL; verbs LH) with a very small functional load; each syllable bears one tone, no contour tones. The only mention of stress is phonetic: VV sequences normally 'receive a single stress with slight temporal length', a few receive 'two stress realizations' and are analysed as two syllables; no statement of where word stress falls, and none that stress is contrastive or absent. Ch. 5 'Kambari word level phonology' (pp. 125-126) concerns only vowel co-occurrence restrictions.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; tone: 'No HH' type gaps are not discussed here (only LL, HL, LHL, LLL, LH listed); tone of morphemes may vary in context but 'never the only variation in the phrase' (p. 62)
new_statements.identity_note: Catalog record and existing statement rest on Janie P. Stark 2010, whose description is based on the Tsikimba dialect of Auna town ('Auna Kambari'). John E. Stark 2011 treats all three Kambari co-languages (Cishingini [asg], Tsikimba [kdl], Tsishingini [tsw]) per the SIL archive record; whether it contains a phonology sketch is unknown.
